items.title: Mongabay Kids launches Wild Guardians: A free education initiative to engage children with nature
items.summary: Mongabay Kids has launched Wild Guardians, a free multimedia educational series that connects upper elementary students with nature and inspires them to become stewards of wild things and wild places. Wild Guardians features stories of children and young people around the world working to protect their favorite animals and ecosystems. Through fun five-minute-long videos, illustrated comics and standards-aligned lessons and activities for fourth and fifth graders, Wild Guardians aims to bridge the gap between storytelling and environmental stewardship. The series features three different conservation topics: Restoring habitat for giraffes in Tanzania, the colorful world of wild bees and exploring and protecting waterways in Tennessee, U.S. Here are the adventures Wild Guardians takes children on: Growing food for giants Follow a group of primary school students in Tanzania who are growing food for giraffes and their community. Children will learn about how they can support their own local wildlife through tree planting, cleanups and habitat restoration. Exploring and protecting waterways Elementary students in Chattanooga, Tennessee, explore their local creek and watershed, home to wildlife such as the hellbender and crawfish. Children will learn that waterways connect landscapes, from mountains to sea, how human activities affect freshwater ecosystems and what they can do to help care for local waterways and the wildlife that depend on them. Discovering wild bees Students learn that there are more 20,000 species of bees, most of them wild bees that don’t produce honey.…
items.t: Mongabay Kids launches Wild Guardians: A free education initiative to engage children with nature

items.title: Longer droughts threaten floating health clinics as Amazon streams run dry
items.summary: RIO BRANCO, Brazil — The sun rises as the riverine healthcare crew starts disembarking medical supplies. They pass down boxes and coolers of all sizes from boat to canoe to smaller canoe, from the far end of the ship to the water’s edge, where a staff member with mud halfway up their shin will hand the load to the next on dry land to carry it uphill where the rest of the team is setting up today’s medical outpost. Every year, doctors, nurses, dentists and community health agents sail along Riozinho do Rôla, delivering medical care to the riverine population of the rural area of Rio Branco, capital of Acre state, in the Brazilian Amazon. Barro Alto, where the fleet is docked, is the first stop. Across the Amazon, a landscape of forests and rivers poses unique obstacles for accessing healthcare. “There are technical and operational challenges that are characteristic to this region,” nurse Alexandra Fernandes, who oversaw this year’s edition of Rio Branco’s healthcare flotilla, told Mongabay. In riverine communities like Barro Alto, isolated for months during wintertime floods, waterbound medical attention becomes a lifeboat. But with climate change and increasingly extreme drought seasons, channels that once connected people to the care they needed are now turning into barriers, as water gives way to mud. According to the November bulletin of the Drought and Immobility Risk in the Amazon Basin report, river levels across the Brazilian Amazon are “below or far below average.” In Acre alone, six of its 22…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Longer droughts threaten floating health clinics as Amazon streams run dry

items.title: China’s mangroves have bounced back. Birds have returned too
items.summary: Between 1998 and 2020, mangrove cover in China more than doubled, while the number of bird species recorded in those areas rose from 148 to 397, according to findings published in The Innovation. The recovery follows decades of steep decline: China lost nearly 70% of its mangroves between 1950 and 1990. Since then, the government has set aside mangrove reserves and restored degraded areas, including former aquaculture ponds. Rising temperatures and increased rainfall have also favored mangrove growth, according to the researchers. Image courtesy of Yang et al., 2026 (CC BY 4.0). The additional forest offers birds more nesting and roosting sites, and may have boosted populations of fish and other aquatic organisms on which many birds feed. The number of globally threatened bird species recorded in China’s mangrove habitats rose from 11 to 21 over the study period. Not all birds stand to benefit as the forests mature. Sandpipers and plovers feed on exposed mudflats and in openings among the trees. Both may become scarcer as mangroves grow denser. Elsewhere, too, mangroves are reclaiming lost ground. A study published in Science in June found that the world’s mangroves had been expanding since around 2010, offsetting much of the loss of the preceding decades. A separate assessment by Global Mangrove Watch found a net increase of 477 square kilometers (184 square miles) between 1985 and 2025 — a modest gain of 0.3% over four decades. Much of the new forest has grown without anyone planting a tree. Banner image: Mangroves…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: China’s mangroves have bounced back. Birds have returned too

items.title: A wake-up call for the UK government on wild birds | Letter
items.summary:
Emma Phipps of SongBird Survival writes that the government must act now to save woodland and farmland species from extinction

The Office for Environmental Protection’s finding that government departments are breaking the law by failing to protect wild birds should alarm us all (UK government ‘breaking the law’ by not stopping decline of wild birds, 18 November).

The scale of bird declines in the UK is impossible to ignore, and songbirds are among the worst affected. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs’ wild bird indicators show that nearly 70% of farmland songbird species have declined since 1970. Woodland songbirds are faring little better, with more than 30% of species in decline. Unfortunately, none of this comes as a surprise. Decades of monitoring by scientists and dedicated volunteers have shown that our wild birds are in trouble. Yet successive governments have failed to act with the urgency needed to halt these declines.

Continue reading...
items.t: A wake-up call for the UK government on wild birds | Letter

items.title: In South Africa’s Limpopo, residents wonder what the next flood will bring
items.summary: “Everyone needs to understand their responsibilities before an emergency occurs.” This is the view of Hope Magidimisha, a national planning commissioner in the Office of the Presidency, South Africa. She said the January floods in South Africa’s Limpopo province, which is still feeling the effects, should serve as a reminder that disaster preparedness must begin long before heavy rains arrive. Some residents affected by the floods are still uncertain whether the repairs carried out since January will protect them when the next floods come. In Boelang, about 15 kilometers (9.3 miles) southwest of Ba-Phalaborwa, a municipality in Limpopo’s Mopani district, residents are once again fetching municipal water from their taps after infrastructure damaged by the January floods was repaired in March. Shanine (not her real name, due to safety concerns) told Mongabay that the repairs restored their water supply after the community had gone without municipal water for almost three months. However, she said water pressure remained unreliable, with water sometimes flowing slowly. “Our water infrastructure is right in the Selati River. The municipality has repaired it, but we are not sure how safe the structure is to withstand another flood,” she said. The January floods left a trail of destruction in Limpopo and disrupted learners from attending school and severely damaged water infrastructure in Boelang village. Two main pipelines crossing the Selati River at Boelang were washed away, while a pump station also failed. The damage left residents without municipal water for almost three…
items.t: In South Africa’s Limpopo, residents wonder what the next flood will bring

items.title: Analysis: The collapse of UN climate talks, over fossil fuels, was years in the making
items.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — Going into this year’s U.N. climate talks in Turkey, expectations were notably low. Still, the outcome was even worse than expected—a failure to reach an overall agreement at a time of frequent extreme weather events fueled by climate change. While negotiations collapsed over one main point of contention—whether to include language about fossil fuels, the main driver of global warming—this fight over this has been building for many years. During previous conferences, nations frequently threatened to walk away if there wasn’t a strong agreement on fossil fuels. Instead, in the end, they voiced their disagreements in closing plenaries and ultimately got in line. This time, many countries were not willing to do that. By Peter Prengaman, Associated Press Banner image: The Jeffrey Energy Center coal-fired power plant operates at sunset near Emmett, Kansas., Jan. 3, 2026, in Topeka, Kansas. Charlie Riedel, Associated PressThis article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Analysis: The collapse of UN climate talks, over fossil fuels, was years in the making

items.title: Talk of scrapping Natural England smacks of a government not joining the dots
items.summary:
Environmentalists say abolishing independent body will make it easier for landowners and developers ‘to trash nature’

Not just any quango, Natural England is the only public body that exists to legally protect the jewels in the crown of English nature – places increasingly under threat in a country that is overseeing an ongoing and devastating decline in its natural world.

Ecologists who work for Natural England are independent, and have the legal duty to scrutinise political decisions and ensure that short-term gallops for growth are not allowed to bulldoze forever rare and declining habitats.

Continue reading...
items.t: Abolishing Natural England would be travesty, say campaigners

items.title: Colombia president’s move on mining, oil weakens country’s Amazon protections, experts warn
items.summary: Colombia’s government, led by far-right President Abelardo De la Espriella, has sought to distance itself from the environmental policies of his 2022-2026 predecessor, left-wing Gustavo Petro, including those affecting the Amazon. The new administration in Bogotá recently repealed Resolution 0961, which prohibited large-scale mining and hydrocarbon extraction in this region, a move that experts say weakens protections not only for the biome but also for the Indigenous peoples who sustain it. The Ministry of Environment argues that the resolution was repealed because it was enacted without prior consultation with the region’s Afro-Colombian, Raizal and Palenquero traditional communities, and the measure does not, by itself, guarantee the Amazon biome’s protection. However, experts consulted by Mongabay say that, beyond repealing a measure — which was not the only one protecting the Amazon — the decision is also a political gesture that casts doubt on Colombia’s hard-won leadership in environmental protection. Organizations say that despite this leadership role, fossil fuel extraction and its infrastructure have accelerated forest loss in the Colombian Amazon, paving the way for other industries such as logging, mining and agriculture. A 2025 report by Earth Insight, the International Institute for Sustainable Development (IISD) and the National Organization of Indigenous Peoples of the Colombian Amazon (OPIAC) warns that 14 million hectares (34.6 million acres) of oil and gas blocks cover 28% of the Colombian Amazon — with 8 million hectares (19.8 million acres) overlapping…
items.t: Colombia president’s move on mining, oil weakens country’s Amazon protections, experts warn

items.title: ‘We had to reinvent the system completely,’ Brazilian philanthropy leader says
items.summary: In November 2025, Indigenous and Afro-descendent peoples, frontline defenders and civil society movements mobilized in unprecedented numbers in Belém, Brazil, to advocate for their demands at the 30th U.N. Climate Change Conference (COP30). One of the key demands was for direct access to climate finance. At COP30, donors announced a new $1.8 billion pledge to support Indigenous peoples’ and Afro-descendent and local communities’ land tenure and resource rights. However, despite certain advances in climate finance and philanthropy, major bottlenecks still remain a year later when it comes to implementation of such commitments. For example, under the previous $1.7 billion pledge, only 7.2% of the funds in 2025 went directly to Indigenous and community organizations, with the vast majority routed through international NGOs, consultancies and development banks. “That system is ill-designed and it is trapping the money. We know what we need. We have the systems and we don’t want anybody else in the middle creating these layers,” Maria Amália Souza, Fundo Casa Socioambiental’s founder and director of Global Philanthropy Strategies, tells Mongabay. “We can attend to the demands of our societies, our movements and our causes much better because we belong to them. The belonging is the part that nobody else can claim.” Determined to not replicate the shortcomings of conventional philanthropy, Souza gathered community and movement leaders at Fundo Casa Socioambiental, a Brazilian socio-environmental fund established in 2005, to design a system to rapidly redistribute funds through…
items.t: ‘We had to reinvent the system completely,’ Brazilian philanthropy leader says

items.title: Kiwi Birds Are Finally Returning To The Wild Around Wellington Thanks To This Conservation Project
items.summary:
For around 150 years, the hills surrounding Wellington, New Zealand, were missing one very special sound: the call of a wild kiwi. These unusual birds, among the country’s most recognizable national symbols, disappeared from the area generations ago. But now, thanks to an ambitious conservation effort, they’re finally making a comeback.

Behind this success is the Capital Kiwi Project, founded by conservationist Paul Ward. Through years of predator control and cooperation with local communities, the project has helped bring kiwi back to the wild landscapes surrounding New Zealand’s capital, where the birds are once again living and breeding freely.

Scroll down to check out how the project moved along and read more about how it got to the point of reinstating a beloved native species.

More info: capitalkiwi.co.nz | Instagram | Facebook | youtube.com 

Before kiwi could return to Wellington’s hills, the Capital Kiwi Project had to tackle one of the biggest threats to their survival: introduced predators 

Capital Kiwi Project 

Trap deployment, Pipinui Point, 2019

Photo by Josiah Watson

Kiwi are unlike most other birds. They’re flightless, mostly nocturnal, and covered in hair-like feathers. They also have long, sensitive beaks with nostrils near the tips, allowing them to sniff out insects, worms, and other food beneath the ground. Found naturally only in New Zealand, these curious-looking birds are also deeply connected to the country’s cultural identity.

Beginning in 2019, the team established a predator-control network that would…
items.t: Kiwi Birds Are Finally Returning To The Wild Around Wellington Thanks To This Conservation Project

items.title: Warming seas threaten South Korea’s iconic squid fishery with collapse by 2040s
items.summary: Rapidly warming sea temperatures and marine heat waves could eliminate South Korea’s domestic catch of the Pacific flying squid by the 2040s, according to a recent study, reports contributor Kelly Kasulis Cho for Mongabay. The Pacific flying squid (Todarodes pacificus) has long been a culturally vital and affordable dietary staple across the Korean peninsula. However, data from South Korea’s national statistics service reveals that current domestic harvest volumes have decreased to just one-sixteenth of levels recorded in 2002. Between 2023 and 2025, prominent national fisheries failed to produce 10% of the annual yield recorded in the peak harvest year of 1999, when the catch reached 225,122 metric tons. Between 2022 and 2026, fresh squid prices surged by more than 40%, according to the Korea Agro-Fisheries & Food Trade Corporation. Over the past decade, sea surface temperatures surrounding the Korean Peninsula rose by 0.7° Celsius (1.26° Fahrenheit), more than double the global average. The study by researchers at Pukyong National University (PKNU) in Busan predicted that South Korea could reach a “zero-catch state” between 2043 and 2048, depending on future global greenhouse gas emissions scenarios. “Long-term warming is making traditional fishing grounds less suitable, while marine heat waves — periods of unusually warm seawater lasting at least five consecutive days — add episodes of intense heat stress,” said Kim Kyung-hoi, corresponding author of the study and ocean engineering professor at PKNU. Kim added that shifts in ocean currents and wind patterns carry…
items.t: Warming seas threaten South Korea’s iconic squid fishery with collapse by 2040s

items.title: From farm to airline plates, a Zambia farm closes its food-waste loop
items.summary: LUSAKA, Zambia — A passenger finishing a salad on a flight out of Lusaka may not know where the vegetables came from — or where some of the organic waste generated during meal preparation ends up. The answer to both questions could be: A 10-hectare (25-acre) farm on the outskirts of Zambia’s capital run by Loctaguna Organics. The farm supplies vegetables and herbs to Newrest Zambia, a catering company that supplies meals to airline companies operating out of Lusaka. Some organic waste from the catering operation is then returned to Loctaguna, where it is used as compost. The farm runs on an agroecology model. Loctaguna produces vegetables, fruits, herbs and animal products without synthetic fertilizers or pesticides, employing 12 people. “The most fundamental part of this whole process is soil health, promoting the soil health,” Loctaguna founder Kanangwa Newlove said. Goats and pigs are part of the Loctaguna Organics ecosystem. The droppings from the livestock are used to produce manure and the residues from the meals are fed to the pigs. Image by Chisapi Kumbutso for Mongabay. Newlove’s journey into agriculture followed a decade-long career in business and marketing. “I used my gratuity from COMACO to set up operations on this farm,” she told Mongabay referring to COMACO Limited, where she worked as a sales and marketing operations manager. Her transition from business to farming has shaped Loctaguna’s approach to connecting organic production with commercial markets. Through a partnership with Kasisi Agricultural Training Centre, she also promotes agroecological farming…
items.t: From farm to airline plates, a Zambia farm closes its food-waste loop

items.title: How a tiny rare frog became an ecological warning sign for Madagascar
items.summary:
The golden mantella is said to be found wherever gold is, making its habitat a target for illegal mining, which is destroying fragile ecosystems across the country

As Albert Rakotoarisoa emerges from the forest into a clearing in Mangabe reserve in the east of Madagascar, he sees dozens of holes dug in the marshy ground, a sign that people have been here to search for gold.

“I came a couple of weeks ago, and these weren’t here,” he says as he surveys the damage, counting 40 holes. “I’m really disappointed.”

items.title: Wolves help wild blueberries grow, US study finds
items.summary: Every summer in northern Minnesota, gray wolves become fruit eaters, mostly. During peak berry season in July and August, berries make up as much as 83% of adult wolves’ weekly diets in the Greater Voyageurs Ecosystem, a southern boreal forest region that borders Canada. Now a new study shows the blueberries also get something out of the deal. Blueberry seeds that passed through a wolf’s gut sprouted faster and more often than seeds taken straight from the fruit, researchers reported in Biology Letters. Gray wolves (Canis lupus) cover long distances quickly, so the authors write that they are likely effective long-distance dispersers of blueberry seeds. The authors say the trip through the gut probably scuffs or chemically wears down the seed coat. The scat may work like fertilizer and protect seeds from pathogens. A wild blueberry (Vaccinium angustifolium) in the Rocky Mountains.  During peak berry season in July and August, berries make up as much as 83% of adult wolves’ weekly diets in some regions. Photo by Eugene Kim via Flickr (CC BY 2.0) “Honestly, we were surprised that gut passage through wolves increased the germination success and speed of blueberry seeds,” lead author Alex Gross told Mongabay in an email. Gross, now a master’s student at Northern Michigan University, did the research with the University of Minnesota’s Voyageurs Wolf Project. Researchers collected fresh wolf scats in 2017 and 2018. They picked out 802 seeds and grew them in petri dishes in a growth chamber for 60 days. Alongside them,…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Wolves help wild blueberries grow, US study finds

items.title: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution
items.summary: Scientists have discovered previously unknown viruses that could help explain how some of life’s earliest biological structures evolved. The surprising findings challenge a longstanding evolutionary theory and suggest that viruses may have hidden capabilities far beyond simply infecting cells.
items.t: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution

items.title: This Page Shared 31 Cats That Look Remarkably Similar To Everyday Foods (New Pics)
items.summary:
Cat owners have a name for the pose where the paws vanish and a cat settles into a neat, rounded block: the loaf. It’s a fair description, and once you start seeing food in your pets, it’s hard to stop. A curled-up ginger becomes a cinnamon roll. A Siamese with dark ears and paws could pass for a toasted marshmallow. A tabby stretched along the sofa has the stripes of a sausage fresh off the grill.

Spotting these lookalikes is the whole idea behind the Instagram page Soft Cat Memes, which places photos of cats next to the foods they could easily be confused with. We featured their first collection  a while ago, and there was no shortage of new ones to choose from. This time, you’ll meet fluffy kittens that resemble ice cream sandwiches and chunky gingers in the exact shade of a chicken nugget.

items.title: Bumblebees are problem-solvers too
items.summary: Turns out bumblebees are spontaneous problem solvers too! In a series of experiments, scientists found that untrained bumblebees were able to find novel solutions to get a reward. The research builds on previous experiments that showed that bumblebees can work as a team and possess cognitive abilities despite their tiny brains. Watch this video to see how bumblebees worked through a hurdle to get to a sweet reward.This article was originally published on Mongabay

items.title: Country diary 1906: Peace reigns again in the deer park
items.summary:
28 November 1906: A month ago the hart roared a deep challenge; now he does not threaten but trots with dignity towards his harem

What a difference a few weeks make to the behaviour of the park stags. A month ago, if approached, the excited hart angrily scraped the ground, swelled his shaggy neck, and, lowering his head, coughed defiance or roared that deep, far-sounding challenge. One felt it wise to give him antler-room and leave him to guard his more nervous hinds. Now, though the great beasts are not so timid as the fallow bucks, he does not threaten, but, standing at gaze, waits until we come near; then, wheeling, he trots with dignity towards his harem, turning occasionally to see if we are following. When we have passed he calmly turns his attention once more to the rough park grass. The hinds are won and the annual battles are over; even the silly fellows have ceased to grunt and run aimlessly amongst the trees; peace reigns in the park until next autumn.

An interesting hedgehog story has been sent to me. At a country house near Malvern the cats are fed out of doors from a large dish. Regularly a wild hedgehog comes to the dish and feeds, unmolested by the cats; probably the well-fed cats look upon the hedgehog as an inhabitant of the garden and not as game. This is curious, but not so strange when we consider what a well-armed animal the hedgehog is. Last week, however, the hedgehog brought with it to the dish a young one, but the cats, probably because they were used to the presence of the mother, did not attack the toothsome…
items.t: Country diary 1906: Peace reigns again in the deer park

items.title: ‘Once installed, there’s no getting rid of it’: what Falklands oil plans mean for its seals, whales and penguins
items.summary:
While Argentina and the UK dispute sovereignty over the islands and its vast oil reserves, environmentalists fear for one of the Atlantic’s richest ecosystems

From the air, the main Falkland Islands form two large, jagged shapes against the South Atlantic. East Falkland and West Falkland are surrounded by 778 smaller islands and islets east of Patagonia’s southern tip.

The archipelago, a British overseas territory claimed by Argentina, is home to large colonies of albatrosses and penguins. Its waters, with those of the Patagonian shelf, provide feeding grounds for sea lions, southern elephant seals and southern right whales.

items.title: Plan to breed rare Asian golden cats for pets raises conservation concerns
items.summary: An Indonesian company has sought to register a captive-breeding facility with the Secretariat of CITES, the global wildlife trade treaty, to commercially breed and export rare Asian golden cats as pets, report Mongabay’s Spoorthy Raman and Fernanda Wenzel. If approved, PT Alam Nusantara Jayatama would become the first facility in the world to commercially breed Asian golden cats (Catopuma temminckii) in captivity for the international pet market. On behalf of Indonesia, the CITES Secretariat issued a public notification in August, granting signatory countries until Nov. 10 to object before the facility is added to the registry of commercial breeding facilities. Classified as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, an estimated 7,000 Asian golden cats remain in the wild, threatened by habitat loss, as well as poaching for their skins and bones. While wild-caught individuals are protected under CITES Appendix I — which bans international commercial trade — captive-bred animals from registered facilities can be legally sold with export permits. According to documents from Indonesia’s Ministry of Forestry to the CITES Secretariat, the facility initiated its breeding program in 2013 using four legally acquired wild-caught Asian golden cats. By 2025, the facility reported its population had grown to 36 individuals across three generations. This rapid reproduction rate and animal welfare standards have come under scrutiny. “They are super challenging to breed,” said Mike Brocklehurst, a carnivore specialist who ran a conservation breeding program for Asian golden cats at Melbourne Zoo…
items.t: Plan to breed rare Asian golden cats for pets raises conservation concerns

items.title: This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s
items.summary: A tiny California trapdoor spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome roughly 50% larger than a human's, despite being only about the size of a quarter. Scientists discovered that its enormous genome contains 4.6 billion DNA base pairs and 52 chromosomes, revealing surprising clues about spider evolution.
items.t: This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s

items.title: Kuala Lumpur otters raise river revival hopes
items.summary: KUALA LUMPUR — Beneath a tangle of highway in the Malaysian capital, a family of otters rolls around in a patch of riverside sand, delighting the few passersby who notice them. Small groups of otters are now being seen regularly in parts of the city, including along the once heavily polluted Klang River. Otters rest on the sandy shore of the Klang River in Kuala Lumpur just south of the city center. Image by Mohd Rasfan / AFP. Theories vary on whether the smooth-coated otters (Lutrogale perspicillata), classed as vulnerable on the Red List of the IUCN, the global wildlife conservation authority, have returned to the city or were hiding in plain sight all along. But their presence has raised hopes that efforts to clean up the Klang may be bearing fruit, and could inspire further improvement. Top: A stork flies past bridges and commercial buildings along the Klang River where smooth-coated otters have been sighted. Bottom: Woo Chee Yoong from the Malaysia Otter Network poses for a photograph with his binoculars used to spot otters along the Klang. Images by Mohd Rasfan / AFP. The Klang was once one of the world’s dirtiest waterways, designated a Class 5 severely polluted river under Malaysia’s rankings, the worst possible rating. Years of work improved it to Class 3, or moderately polluted, which seems to have encouraged the otters to move in, said Malaysian wildlife ecologist Woo Chee Yoong. Otters play along the Klang River, next to plastic waste caught beneath a…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Kuala Lumpur otters raise river revival hopes

items.title: DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why early life may have survived Earth's intense ultraviolet radiation: a key component of DNA appears to turn potentially destructive damage into something easier to repair. The discovery could help solve a decades-old evolutionary mystery and reveal how life endured the harsh conditions of our planet's earliest days.
items.t: DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth

items.title: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA
items.summary: At an astonishing 194 years old, Jonathan the giant tortoise is the world's oldest living land animal, and scientists may have finally uncovered the secrets behind his extraordinary lifespan. Researchers identified 287 unique genetic variants linked to processes that help repair damaged DNA, control inflammation, regulate insulin, and suppress cancer.
items.t: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA

items.title: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along
items.summary: A decades-old theory suggesting that evolution protects its most important genes from mutations has been dealt a major blow. An extensive new analysis of mutations in bacteria and yeast found no evidence that essential genes mutate less frequently than other genes. Researchers say earlier studies may have been misled by harmful mutations that disappeared through natural selection before scientists could detect them.
items.t: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along

items.title: Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite
items.summary: The human family tree may need a major overhaul. New research from Monash University challenges the traditional classification of our ancient ancestors, arguing that species such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus should be grouped within our own genus, Homo. As scientists uncover more fossils and analyze evolutionary relationships, the boundaries that once separated these ancient relatives are becoming increasingly difficult to defend.
items.t: Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite

items.title: ‘People couldn’t deal with watching an animal die’: the strange saga of Timmy the whale – and how a whole country lost its mind
items.summary:
When the humpback got stranded on Germany’s Baltic coast, crowds gathered, conspiracy theorists pitted themselves against scientists and animal lovers argued with vets. Why did the animal trigger such an intense derangement?

What surprised Bodo Köpnick was how loud the whale was. “You could hear it as far away as the next village. It was eerie, but also impressive,” he says, then pauses to think how best to describe the noise a suffering humpback makes at night. “It was like a cow moaning. It went to your marrow.”

Köpnick, 65, is everything you would hope for in a volunteer fire chief on a sleepy holiday island: a grandfatherly figure who mostly spends his weekends teaching local children about health and safety, and letting them climb on the engines. But on 31 March his life was made infinitely more stressful by the appearance of a lost whale that had got itself stranded on the shores of his island of Poel, in northern Germany. It became his fate to stand on the shoreline and guard the huge creature while behind him an entire country lost its mind.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘People couldn’t deal with watching an animal die’: the strange saga of Timmy the whale – and how a whole country lost its mind

items.title: ‘Legally, they don’t exist’: the hybrid crabs puzzling biologists and fishers
items.summary:
A heatwave in the Bering Sea that killed 10bn snow crabs has led to a new hybrid emerging that has no fishing quotas

Somewhere out on the Bering Sea, hundreds of miles off the coast of Alaska, a group of researchers onboard the trawler Alaska Knight haul up a heap of crabs from the seabed. As they sort and measure their haul, something seems wrong.

The catch, which usually features species such as the snow crab – a species of spider crab growing up to a metre wide with its legs outstretched – or its larger relative, the tanner crab, is instead dominated by an odd-looking hybrid of the two species.

items.title: The British island that made a deal with nature
items.summary: LUNDY ISLAND — United Kingdom. Out in the Bristol Channel, nestled between Wales and England, the rugged island of Lundy is one of the UK’s most pioneering conservation stories. From the return of thousands of seabirds to thriving marine life beneath its waves, decades of conservation have helped transform this small island. But Lundy’s story isn’t simply about keeping people out. Local fishermen helped shape the marine protected area, and the UK’s first ever no-take zone was designed alongside the needs of the people who depend on these waters. Today, the island is home to thriving wildlife, a working fishing community and thousands of visitors each year. Mongabay’s Video Team wants to cover questions and topics that matter to you. items.title: Country diary: Watching a garden spider at work – do I detect a personality? | Oliver Southall
items.summary:
Hurstpierpoint, West Sussex: The way that it sits patiently, and solves problems … it’s hard not to wonder if it has some kind of inner life

Three months with a newborn has given me a fresh perspective on nature. What will Tom enjoy out here, I wonder, as we step outside. I hold him under trees and watch his astonished eyes. Every morning, as a hopeful inoculation against arachnophobia, I show him the garden spider (Araneus diadematus) outside our back window. Is that a smile?

Attending to a baby’s developing preferences has got me thinking about what makes an individual creature unique. Recently I learned that Len Howard – whose 1952 book Birds As Individuals lovingly described the quirks of her garden tits and thrushes – lived nearby. Contemporary experiments with honeybees have shown that diversity in workers’ personality traits makes for an adaptable and resilient hive.

items.title: Extreme rainfalls flood Sri Lanka’s coastal city as wetlands, drains vanish
items.summary: COLOMBO — On Nov. 6, a 129-millimeter (5-inch) downpour flooded parts of Sri Lanka’s commercial capital within minutes, stranding commuters and submerging a large number of vehicles. Siva Sivasagunthan, a three-wheeler driver working at a local ride-hailing app, told Mongabay that the water levels quickly increased and his vehicle was partially submerged in water. It took him around two hours to reach a location that would have usually taken 30 minutes to reach on a normal day. The downpour left many Colombo residents panicking. According to Ajith Wijemanna, director of Sri Lanka’s Department of Meteorology, there have been a few instances over the decades when Colombo has experienced rainfall exceeding 400 mm (15.7 in). In June 1992, the city experienced a rainfall of 493.7 mm (19.4 in). In November 2010, a 440.2 mm (17.3 in) rainfall was recorded in 24 hours. Wijemanna told Mongabay that the intensity of the rainfall — the speed of rainfall received in an hour — is extremely important. According to meteorological department readings, the rainfall intensity on Nov. 6 was more than 120 mm (4.7 in) per hour. The rain gauge reading at another location in Colombo indicated more than 135 mm (5.3 in) of rainfall per hour. “We believe that the main cause of flooding was the high intensity during a short period of time, such as an hour, which was similar to a gushing downpour,” Wijemanna said. He noted that Sri Lanka currently lacked technology such as a Doppler radar system to support…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Extreme rainfalls flood Sri Lanka’s coastal city as wetlands, drains vanish

items.title: Autopsy Results Reveal What Really Happened To Fiona The Hippo, As Witnesses Speak Out On Freak Accident
items.summary:
The autopsy results for Fiona the hippo have finally been released, giving more details about what happened inside her body after she swallowed a visitor’s knitted hat. 

The nine-year-old Cincinnati Zoo favorite passed away on November 19, despite her caretakers trying several ways to save her. 

Now, the zoo has shared the findings of her examination, explaining why the veterinary team couldn’t remove the object and why even continued treatment wouldn’t have changed the outcome. 

Autopsy results revealed how the hat became stuck inside Fiona and couldn’t be removed 

On Friday, November 20, Cincinnati Zoo released the results of Fiona’s necropsy, the term for an animal autopsy. 

The examination revealed that the knitted hat had become lodged in the middle of her small intestine . It was approximately 25 feet beyond her final stomach compartment and 50 feet from the end of her intestines. 

This meant the object was stuck in a part of her digestive system the veterinary team could not reach with the equipment available. 

Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden / Youtube

items.title: US leases American Samoan seabed for mining in auction deemed illegal by court
items.summary: The U.S. government has auctioned off 12.7 million hectares (31.5 million acres) of the American Samoan seabed, despite public opposition and a federal court ruling that found the sale to be illegal. The sale marks the first time a country has completed an auction of seabed mineral leases that grant the right to explore for minerals. The auction, which took place on the morning of Nov. 19 in Thousand Oaks, California, was publicly livestreamed, offering two vast lots of American Samoan seabed: One covering about 15 million acres, and the other about 16 million acres. Mongabay attended the livestream. Just two bidders showed up: A U.S. company called Wetstone U.S. Ventures and the Norwegian company Adepth. However, only Wetstone participated in the bidding process. By the end of the auction, which lasted approximately 20 minutes, Wetstone had secured both leases at the starting price of $3 million each, equivalent to approximately 19 U.S. cents per acre. In 2024, American Samoa, a U.S. territory, imposed a moratorium on deep-sea mining in waters extending up to 3 nautical miles from its coastline. The U.S. government has jurisdiction over the remainder of the exclusive economic zone (EEZ), which extends 200 nautical miles from shore, allowing it to pursue seabed mineral activities in this area without approval from the American Samoan government. Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, center, and other activists protesting outside the site of the auction in Thousand Oaks, California. Image by Hunter Ries/Greenpeace USA. In a statement released on Nov. 16, a few days…This article was…

Scientists reared the San Francisco natives through their vulnerable youth before setting them free in nature

San Francisco garter snakes born and raised in a zoo-based conservation program have been released into the wild for the first time as part of an effort to save what is considered one of North America’s most beautiful snakes.

The non-venomous reptiles are known for their striking colors – red heads, turquoise bellies and vibrant red and black stripes on their sides. The species, found only on the San Francisco peninsula, has been listed as endangered for more than half a century.

items.title: Renovated BUGarium in the US aims to connect people and insects
items.summary: For many people a trip to the zoo is an opportunity to see favorite animals like gorillas, giraffes and lions. But in Alburquerque, New Mexico, U.S., visitors can add spiders, scorpions and ants to their must-see list at the ABQ BioPark BUGarium. The facility also includes an aquarium, traditional zoo and botanic garden. The BUGarium was closed for a year and reopened in October 2026 following a $1.45 million renovation. Insects are the largest group of animals on Earth, and ecologically essential as pollinators and the base of many food chains. Famed entomologist E.O. Wilson once said: “If we were to wipe out insects alone — just that group alone — on this planet, which we are trying hard to do, the rest of life and humanity with it would mostly disappear from the land. And within a few months.” The BUGarium exists to educate the public about the importance of insects. “Whether they’re pollinating plants, recycling nutrients, controlling pests, or supporting entire food webs, these animals are essential to healthy ecosystems,” said ABQ BioPark Associate Director Matthew Peterson in a statement. Bugs are not always an easy sell. “Guests come to the BUGarium with a wide spectrum of attitudes ranging from disgust and horror to fascination and awe,” Alexandra Miller, the curator of entomology at the ABQ BioPark told Mongabay in an email. “We hope guests learn how important arthropods are to ecosystems around the world, what they can do to support native populations, and that arthropods require specialized care…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Renovated BUGarium in the US aims to connect people and insects

items.title: Philippine corn farmers investigate links between chemical farming and soil erosion
items.summary: LAKE SEBU, Philippines — To the untrained eye, a handful of soil might appear to be a monotone brown. But to farmer Welna Sumulde, who grew up among generations of Indigenous T’boli farmers on the Philippines island of Mindanao, the slightest change in the color of the soil is a whisper from the land, a warning of its degradation. “Around 2023, we observed changes in our soil. The color became lighter, the leaves looked different, and the cassava we harvest became smaller. We also observed fewer living organisms on our soil,” Samulde told Mongabay. Samulde and other farmers in her community also thought changes in the soil might hold answers to a troubling puzzle: Why do fish keep dying in nearby Lake Sebu, a lake that lies in the natural basin below their upland farms? They said they began to suspect that soil erosion from surrounding corn farms was speeding up siltation in the lake — and that changes in farming practices were accelerating erosion. With the help of NGOs and scientists, the farmers were able to test this hypothesis. MASIPAG Mindanao coordinator Leo XL Fuentes, in yellow, conducts a soil test alongside farmers of the Lem Bulul Farmers Association. The farmers are comparing soil fertility and pH between traditional and chemical corn farms. Image by Geela Garcia for Mongabay. items.t: Philippine corn farmers investigate links between chemical farming and soil erosion

items.title: Indigenous protesters board soy and oil barges on Brazilian Amazon river
items.summary: Hundreds of Indigenous protesters on several small boats and canoes stopped and boarded barges carrying soybeans and fuel on Brazil’s Tapajós River in the eastern Amazon. The demonstrations on Nov. 14 and 15 were to demand protection for the river amid industrial expansion and legal recognition of Indigenous territories in the region. The two-day demonstration near Santarém, in Pará state, drew more than 650 protesters. “Our children need this river, just as we need this river,” Jackson Tapajós, executive secretary of the Tupinambá Indigenous Council who participated in the protest, told Mongabay by phone. Smoke in the air from nearby forest fires was so thick that protesters could not see the barges approach until they were close, he said. Indigenous women negotiated with armed security guards after approaching the fuel barge on Nov. 14, explaining that the group was peacefully protesting. The guards allowed them to board but stayed with them, Tapajós told Mongabay. “We managed to talk to some of these guards … but they were by our side the whole time, the whole time with their guns, so that creates a lot of tension,” Tapajós said. The Tapajós River is an export artery for the region, carrying large amounts of soybeans and corn from Brazil’s agricultural heartland to ports on the Amazon River, which ultimately connect to international trade routes via the Atlantic. According to the Ministry of Ports and Airports, 16.8 million metric tons of cargo was moved through the waterway in 2025, up 14.3% from 2024.…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Indigenous protesters board soy and oil barges on Brazilian Amazon river

items.title: It’s time to put Africa’s forest communities on the map (commentary)
items.summary: The U.N. General Assembly’s recent adoption of a new standard world map, more accurately reflecting the true size of Africa than depicted in the Eurocentric 16th-century Mercator projection, is great news and a welcome reminder that multilateralism isn’t dead yet. It also doesn’t tell the whole story. We’re not talking about how the continent was carved up between the former colonial powers through such events as the Berlin conference of 1884-1885, though the social, economic and political impacts of the often straight and artificial lines drawn on those maps are still felt today. No, we’re talking about how maps of Central African states are still used by foreign interests and political elites as tools to perpetuate power — with control of natural resources and the benefits they generate tending to flow outwards and upwards — rather than to the people living in these areas. Resource map of the Congo Basin. Graphic courtesy of Earth Insight. Today, much of the Congo Basin, the world’s second largest rainforest, resembles a patchwork of extractive industry concessions, strictly protected areas and an ever-increasing array of carbon offset projects which our organization has documented. These have largely failed to stem deforestation and biodiversity loss, while delivering few or no benefits to local populations, and in many cases, causing severe impacts on human rights and food security. What maps typically don’t show are the systems of longstanding customary rights and usage by Indigenous and local communities (IPLCs) that extend across the vast region, and which…
items.t: It’s time to put Africa’s forest communities on the map (commentary)

items.title: Where family foundations can help marine conservation
items.summary: COP17 ended in Armenia amid disappointment over the lack of concrete measures to reduce biodiversity loss by 2030. Finance was a sore point. Philanthropy is only a small part of that picture, but foundations can take risks that public agencies often cannot. I think there are some particularly good opportunities for smaller foundations in marine conservation. My intended audience is family foundations that give away perhaps $2 million to $15 million a year and have a handful of staff. Over the summer I went through the academic literature and Mongabay’s coverage in English, Spanish, and Portuguese to see what the evidence actually shows about marine conservation outcomes in the Americas. A first summary of that assessment – “From paper parks to lasting protection, here’s what works in marine conservation” – appeared last month. In some cases Mongabay’s reporting helped me understand why the results of a study were so disappointing. Our reporters had spoken to the people responsible for managing these areas, as well as people who lived or fished in them. In reading about some of these places, I was struck by how long the laws protecting them had been on the books. Some of the agencies responsible for enforcing those laws lack adequate funding. Elsewhere, the designation of a protected area was done with little regard for the people who fished there. A school of mobula rays off Mexico. Image by Rhett Ayers Butler Making existing protected areas work I suspect it’s easier to raise money to establish…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Where family foundations can help marine conservation

items.title: Ecuador copper mine advancing despite opposition from Indigenous communities
items.summary: A proposed copper mine on Indigenous land in southeastern Ecuador is getting closer to opening despite opposition from some Shuar communities, who say they reject the project altogether and don’t want to participate in talks with the government. The Warintza mine received environmental authorization this year, and officials will now begin meeting with Indigenous communities about how the project, if constructed, would impact their way of life. But some community members don’t want to be consulted at all, and say they’re worried about relocation from the territory. “We want absolutely nothing to do with mining,” one community member, who asked to remain anonymous due to fear for his personal safety, told Mongabay. “And we don’t even want to be consulted.” If the project moves forward, Lowell Mineral Exploration Ecuador S.A., a subsidiary of Solaris Resources, would extract copper for around 22 years from approximately 8,660 hectares (21,399 acres) across six concessions. It would also extract molybdenum concentrates and some gold and silver. A soccer game in the center of the Maikiuaints community. Image by Brandi Morin/Survival International. Construction would clear more than 2,025 hectares (5,003 acres) of primary forest and divert the Warints and Piuntz rivers, critical to Indigenous communities’ way of life, according to the environmental impact assessment, which received technical approval in April. It could irreversibly change the landscape in some places even after the mine is closed, the assessment said. Surface water and groundwater quality also face high risk,…
items.t: Ecuador copper mine advancing despite opposition from Indigenous communities

items.title: Could a short tail mean a new monkey species in Laos? Some scientists think so
items.summary: There is no body. No genetic evidence — yet. There are just photos, but some scientists say those photos show a distinct enough primate to declare it a new species: the short-tailed langur, or Trachypithecus brevicaudus. The proposed species was described in the Vietnamese Journal of Primatology and lives in the Annamite Mountains of Laos. “A photograph of a langur, published by the Saola Foundation, caught my attention because the animal’s tail is noticeably shorter than that of any other species within this group of limestone langurs,” said Tilo Nadler, lead author of the paper and a wildlife consultant for the Vietnamese government and various NGOs. This photo led Nadler and colleagues to investigate. They traveled to the area, a remote set of limestone karsts in Bolikhamxai province in central Laos, and took their own photos. “The first time I observed a group of these langurs, it was immediately clear to me that they were different from all the other limestone langurs I had previously encountered and knew well,” Nadler told Mongabay in an email interview. “It was a very exciting experience.” Male short-tailed langur of a group. Image by Tilo Nadler. But not all scientists agree that these photos prove a new-to-science species. “It could well be a new species, but I think the data that have been presented do not give sufficient support for this,” said primate expert Vincent Nijman, director of EcoVerde Global Consulting, who wasn’t involved with the paper. items.t: Could a short tail mean a new monkey species in Laos? Some scientists think so

items.title: Quechua community in Peru builds up Andean bear camera trap project on their own reserve
items.summary: Maribel Pacco grins as she recalls the first time she saw an Andean bear close-up in the wild. At the forest edge, a mother and her cubs browsed on bromeliads while the volunteer ranger watched for hours in awe. “I’m not a biologist, but at that moment, I decided to become a conservationist,” she says. Today, Pacco leads a camera-trap project to estimate bear numbers and movements in Pumataki, a private community-owned reserve in the buffer zone of Manu National Park, in southeastern Peru. With the help of her Indigenous Quechua community of Pillco Grande, the project has generated some of the first local records of Andean bears (Tremarctos ornatus) in Pumataki. So far, they have identified 10 individual Andean bears, distinguishable by the unique pattern of facial markings. Though modest and only 3 years old, information gathered from the camera traps helps inform a Quechua-language environmental education program for youth and is shared at community meetings to highlight the area’s biodiversity. “In the last few years, I’ve seen a lot more involvement of women in Andean bear conservation which is fantastic to see,” said Rebecca Zug, a professor of biology at the Universidad San Francisco de Quito, who is not involved in the project. “There is also so much more power in Indigenous communities building conservation from within and learning about their own biodiversity from someone like Maribel than in having an outside voice come in.” For now, limited funding has forced the project to scale back some of…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Quechua community in Peru builds up Andean bear camera trap project on their own reserve

items.title: UN climate talks slammed by activists, leaders as fossil fuels go unmentioned in draft agreement
items.summary: ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — Negotiators are still seeking concrete commitments for nations to transition away from fossil fuels, as this year’s U.N. climate summit reaches its final day. Friday marks the official end of this year’s two-week summit, known as COP31, which so far has failed to advance the drastic emission cuts needed to avert the most catastrophic effects of climate change. Negotiators in Turkey expect the talks to go into overtime on Saturday. Civil society groups have warned this year’s summit runs the risk of being the “worst COP ever” if fossil fuels don’t make it into the final agreement. By Suzan Fraser, Anton L. items.summary:
The war between the US, Israel and Iran has turned the strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s busiest oil shipping routes, into a battlefield, but also the centre of a deepening environmental disaster. Tankers struck by missiles or sea mines are leaking oil into the Gulf, leaving vast slicks visible from space, staining coastlines and threatening lasting damage to marine ecosystems. Many of these areas remain inaccessible because of the naval blockade, making it virtually impossible to document the devastation on the ground. The Guardian has examined dozens of satellite images and spoken to environmental experts in an effort to assess the scale of the damage

items.summary:
A child’s visit to Cincinnati Zoo on November 8 took an alarming turn for one of the habitat’s best-known residents, leaving her in need of round-the-clock supervision. 

Fiona , the beloved nine-year-old hippo whose premature birth and remarkable survival captured hearts around the world in 2017, swallowed a knitted item thrown into her enclosure by the young guest. 

What initially appeared to be something the animal might overcome without difficulty has since developed into a more concerning situation, with her appetite beginning to decline and raising concerns among her veterinary team. 

As specialists explore ways to help Fiona pass the object naturally, her caregivers have turned to an unconventional piece of equipment in the hope of aiding her recovery. 

Zookeepers try an unusual recovery method as beloved hippo remains under close veterinary watch 

cincinnatizoo/Instagram 

According to zoo spokeswoman Michelle Curley, a kid’s knitted hat became caught in a ceiling fan as they tossed it before being propelled through a small opening above the viewing windows and into Fiona’s enclosure. 

Fiona swallowed the item, although she did not initially show any signs of discomfort. 

In a video update shared by the zoo on November 17, a member of the veterinary staff explained that they had expected the relatively small object to pass through her digestive system. 

However, that did not happen as anticipated. 

cincinnatizoo/Instagram

items.t: “Rooting For Her”: Cincinnati Zoo Updates Public On Fiona The Hippo After She Swallowed A Child’s Knitted Hat

items.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins
items.summary: A new study has uncovered a surprising concern hiding in popular plant-based foods and drinks. Researchers tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk, and soy milk, and found that every single one contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin. Known as mycotoxins, these naturally occurring compounds can contaminate grains, legumes, and seeds during farming and storage.
items.t: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins

items.title: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history
items.summary: A bizarre whale that lived roughly 6 million years ago had a face so dramatically crooked that scientists believe it may have been the most asymmetrical of any mammal. Discovered in Peru, the extinct pygmy sperm whale Scaphokogia huachafo had an enormous downward-curving snout and a skull so distorted that researchers initially thought it had been damaged after death. Instead, its strange anatomy appears to have been an extraordinary evolutionary adaptation for hunting along the seafloor.
items.t: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history

items.title: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs
items.summary: Scientists have discovered a strange bacterium hiding beneath the skin of deep-sea creatures known as sea pigs, revealing an unexpected biological partnership. The microbe has an unusually tiny genome, yet more than a quarter of its DNA is devoted to making surface proteins, some of them exceptionally large. Researchers suspect it depends heavily on its host for survival, but what the sea pigs gain in return remains a mystery.
items.t: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs

items.title: Britain’s birds stay closer to home amid mild winters
items.summary:
Smaller species such as swallows and skylarks are more likely to stay near breeding grounds rather than migrate

Bonfire Night is over, Christmas is coming, and Britain’s birds are getting ready for the winter. They must survive the extremes of our weather and make it through to next spring to get the chance to breed again.

Birds have very different strategies to prepare for cold weather. Many smaller birds – swallows and swifts, cuckoos and chats, warblers and flycatchers – simply avoid it by migrating: some fly all the way to sub-Saharan Africa, where they enjoy the benefits of a second spring and summer south of the equator. Others, such as blackbirds and robins, stay put. But if they sense that a cold spell is coming, they too will head south, though not as far – most either remain in south-west Britain or cross the Channel to France or Spain.

items.t: Britain’s birds stay closer to home amid mild winters

items.title: Meet Phil, the bar-tailed godwit tracked on a 6,800-mile round trip to Siberia
items.summary:
Scientists use lightweight tracker to map wading bird’s extraordinary migration from Norfolk to the Arctic and back

A bar-tailed godwit called Phil has completed a 6,800-mile journey from Norfolk to Siberia and back again, in the first UK mapping of the endurance feats of this long-distance migrant.

A wading bird not much larger than a pigeon, the bar-tailed godwit is known for making the longest recorded non-stop migratory flight of any bird. Populations that visit Britain spend summers breeding in the Arctic Circle before retreating to the unfrozen wetlands of Britain in winter. In 2022, one bar-tailed godwit made the longest recorded non-stop flight, 13,560km over 11 days from Alaska to Tasmania.

items.t: Meet Phil, the bar-tailed godwit tracked on a 6,800-mile round trip to Siberia

items.title: This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs
items.summary: More than 300 million years ago, long before dinosaurs roamed Earth, the Chicago area was a steamy, swampy landscape teeming with bizarre creatures. Now, scientists at the Field Museum have identified a previously unrecognized species of ancient amphibian ancestor, revealing new clues about the evolution of frogs and salamanders.
items.t: This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs
